Drift benchmark source

Source: R/dsg_benchmark.R
dsg_source.Rd

Creates a data source with controlled real and virtual drift, following the pipeline of Hinder et al. (2026), "Real vs. Virtual Drift: Creating Realistic Stream Learning Benchmarks". A source combines nv feature distributions (virtual drift states, given by samplers) with nr labelling rules (real drift states, given by labelers), so it has nv * nr concepts. Moving between two concepts that share the labelling rule is pure virtual drift; moving between two that share the feature distribution is pure real drift.

Most users will create sources with dsg_source_data() (from a real-world stream) or with the synthetic generators dsg_sea(), dsg_agrawal(), dsg_sine() and dsg_mixed(), draw samples with dsg_take(), induce drift with dsg_drift(), and build whole streams with dsg_stream().

Usage

dsg_source(
  samplers,
  labelers,
  real_drift_level = 0.01,
  virtual_p_value = 0.001,
  test_size = 1000,
  n_perm = 2500,
  max_tries = 100
)

Arguments

samplers

List of functions; samplers[[v]](n) returns a data frame (or matrix) with up to n rows drawn from feature distribution v. It may return fewer rows; dsg_take() calls it again until it has enough.

labelers

List of functions; labelers[[r]](x) returns one label per row of the data frame x according to labelling rule r.

real_drift_level

Smallest share of labels that a real drift must change (on test_size points) to be accepted.

virtual_p_value

Largest p-value of the kernel two-sample test (dsg_mmd_test()) for a virtual drift to be accepted.

test_size

Number of points drawn to verify each drift.

n_perm

Number of permutations of the two-sample test.

max_tries

Number of candidate concepts tried by dsg_drift() before it falls back to the strongest real drift found.

Value

dsg_source object

References

Hinder, F., Brinkrolf, J., Lammers, K., and Hammer, B. (2026). Real vs. Virtual Drift: Creating Realistic Stream Learning Benchmarks. In Proceedings of the European Symposium on Artificial Neural Networks, Computational Intelligence and Machine Learning (ESANN 2026), 133-138.

Examples

# Two feature distributions and two labelling rules: four concepts.
source <- dsg_source(
  samplers = list(
    function(n) data.frame(x = stats::runif(n, 0, 1)),
    function(n) data.frame(x = stats::runif(n, 0.5, 1.5))
  ),
  labelers = list(
    function(x) as.integer(x$x > 0.5),
    function(x) as.integer(x$x > 1)
  ),
  test_size = 200, n_perm = 200
)
set.seed(1)
stream <- dsg_stream(source, "-v-r", batch_size = 100)
stream$segments
#>   segment type drift virtual_state real_state p_value label_change
#> 1       1    -     0             2          2      NA           NA
#> 2       2    v     1             1          2       0           NA
#> 3       3    -     0             1          2      NA           NA
#> 4       4    r     2             1          1      NA        0.475
